briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon. Welcome to the climate briefing for September 1, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Worsening Global Climate Disasters and Demands for a Just Transition
sections.content: Today's most significant news concerns the large-scale flood disaster in Nepal. The death toll has now exceeded 1,000 people, 65,000 are in urgent need of relief, and recovery costs are estimated to reach 7 trillion KRW [1, 9, 18, 21, 100, 101, 135]. The Prime Minister of Nepal characterized these floods as a climate change-induced disaster, officially demanding compensation from major greenhouse gas emitters such as the United States, China, and India, and urging active responses from the international community [1, 4, 10, 11, 12, 13, 24, 29, 103, 118, 129, 130, 137, 139]. Concurrently, numerous other climate disaster cases are being reported, including heavy snowfall in Chile's Atacama Desert [5], record-breaking heatwaves in Germany [26], extreme heat and floods across the United States [108], and wildfires, floods, and droughts in Canada, all signaling a global intensification of the climate crisis [133, 136, 138].

sections.title: 🌍 International Trends in Climate Policy, Finance, and Legal Responsibility
sections.content: The issue of legal and financial responsibility for damages caused by climate change is gaining international prominence. Nepal is demanding climate justice by seeking compensation from greenhouse gas-emitting nations for a 'crisis we did not create' [29, 103]. Furthermore, the legal accountability of fossil fuel companies is increasingly emphasized, with new climate change lawsuits, such as those seeking damages from oil companies, being brought before the Supreme Court [117, 131, 132]. However, challenges in advancing climate policies persist, as evidenced by the blocking of New York State's groundbreaking Climate Change Superfund Act [106, 109, 122]. The European Environment Agency (EEA) warns that some parts of Europe may become unsuitable for agriculture due to climate change, while globally, disaster costs resulting from climate change and uncontrolled urban development exceed 600 trillion KRW annually [15, 114, 134].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Domestic Carbon Neutrality Efforts and Institutional Progress
sections.content: Domestically, efforts to strengthen the institutional foundation for climate change response and implement practical carbon neutrality measures are ongoing. The 'Climate Change Center' has changed its corporate name to the 'Climate Change Foundation' after 18 years, seeking to enhance its public role and strengthen cooperation [2, 3, 17, 27]. Various local governments, including Gangneung City, Seongju County, and Jinju City, are conducting education to strengthen climate crisis response and carbon neutrality capabilities, and are encouraging citizen participation by promoting carbon neutrality point subscriptions, clothing resource sharing services, home gardening, and other diverse practical initiatives [23, 35, 36, 37, 39, 40, 49, 50, 52, 55, 56, 58]. Furthermore, Korea Southern Power (KOSPO) is accelerating support for business transitions for small and medium-sized enterprises in the coal sector to help them achieve carbon neutrality [38, 45, 47, 53, 59], and financial support for carbon neutrality is expanding, with 'transition finance' and 'green government bonds' now included in legislation [43].

sections.title: 🌱 Accelerating the Expansion of Renewable Energy and Green Hydrogen
sections.content: According to the government's 2027 budget proposal, the Ministry of Climate's budget has been allocated 25.7 trillion KRW, an 18.3% increase from the previous year, with 2.8 trillion KRW earmarked for expanding the power grid and renewable energy [62, 72, 73, 99]. The government has set a target of 100 GW of renewable energy by 2030 and announced that the state will take responsibility from site selection, demonstrating a strong commitment to expanding renewable energy supply [75]. Notably, there are plans to expand solar power generation in idle spaces along roads and rivers, and 'agrivoltaics,' which allow farmers to generate and sell electricity while farming, are gaining attention as key to achieving the 155 GW solar power target [63, 79, 78, 92, 94]. In Jeju, the first domestic commercial Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) case occurred where wind power electricity is directly supplied to a green hydrogen production facility, marking a significant advancement towards ushering in the era of green hydrogen [88, 91, 95, 96, 97, 98]. Corporate efforts to utilize renewable energy are also diversifying, with Samsung Electronics encouraging appliance usage during periods of abundant renewable energy generation, and YG Entertainment incorporating renewable energy into its concerts [70, 84, 86, 87].

briefing.closing: Today's briefing highlighted the severity of the climate crisis and the efforts of both the international community and domestic stakeholders to address it. This is a critical time when sustained attention and action on climate change are more important than ever. This concludes the climate briefing for September 1, 2026.
